clue.text: Dull doctor: "What's coming on Monday?"

parts.note: DR is the usual abbreviation for doctor
the puzzle ran just before Monday 1 January, so what is coming is the new year: a year, made new

explanation.surface: A boring doctor asks what is on the agenda for Monday.
explanation.walkthrough: This is the puzzle's theme: the puzzle appeared just before Monday 1 January, and the 'new' of New Year is the unwritten signal to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreary and dull are synonyms, both describing something tedious and lacking in interest.

clue.text: Unproductive day after upturn implies decline

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for day

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning a word up means reading it from bottom to top

parts.note: poor land or work is unproductive

explanation.surface: A slack day after a business upturn hints at a coming slump.
explanation.walkthrough: D comes first because the day follows the turned-up word only in the clue's order of mention; the reversed POOR is placed after D.
explanation.definitionFit: To droop is to sag or sink downward, a verb sense matching decline as in falling away.

clue.text: Something added in aspect of awkward encounter when out with new girlfriend?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an addition, such as a new room on a house

definitions.text: aspect of awkward encounter when out with new girlfriend
definitions.meaning: second, punning meaning: the strain felt on bumping into a former partner, split as two words

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the pun: read the answer as EX TENSION, the tension when your ex sees you out with someone new.
explanation.definitionFit: An extension is an added part, like an annexe built onto a house or extra time granted.

clue.text: What's coming on Monday? Not a whisky

indicators.note: 'not a' tells you to drop the letter A from what precedes

parts.note: the new year arrives on Monday, and a new year is a year with its letters remade

explanation.surface: Someone asks what Monday brings and is told: not whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: The theme again: the new YEAR means its letters are rearranged; take away the A and the remaining three give the spirit. 'Not a whisky' looks like a denial but holds the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Rye is whisky distilled chiefly from rye grain, popular in North America.

clue.text: Reckon what's coming on Monday will have daughter deceived

parts.note: to bet is to reckon, as in 'I bet it rains'
the new year starts on Monday, a year made new
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: Someone expects Monday's events to leave their daughter misled.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'new' of New Year is the unwritten signal to rearrange YEAR, here as RAYE.
explanation.definitionFit: To be betrayed is to be let down or misled by someone trusted, so deceived fits.

clue.text: British scientist's marriage not initially attracting people of fashion

indicators.note: 'not initially' asks for the first letter to be left off

parts.note: a wedding is a marriage ceremony
the ton is an old term for fashionable society

explanation.surface: A British scientist's wedding fails to draw the fashionable crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is possessive because the clue's 's links it to the rest: read it as 'British scientist is'. Arthur Eddington was the astrophysicist who confirmed Einstein's light-bending prediction in 1919.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Arthur Eddington was an English astronomer and physicist, an example of a British scientist.

clue.text: Again consolidated agreement to put in thatching

indicators.note: putting something in a material means setting it inside that word

parts.note: reed is a traditional thatching material
a compact is a formal agreement or pact

explanation.surface: A deal is renewed to have a roof thatched.
explanation.definitionFit: To recompact is to compress or pack firmly once more, so it means consolidated again.

clue.text: Long period of time that's new? (and a hint to eight other clues)

parts.note: a year is a period of time
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A long stretch of time that feels fresh, with a note on the puzzle's theme.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket points to the theme: YEAR with N, the new year, is what eight other clues build in as 'what's coming on Monday'.
explanation.definitionFit: To long for something is to yearn for it; both verbs mean to desire intensely.

clue.text: Plague — about to flee? Not entirely a sign of stupidity

indicators.note: not entirely means leaving off part of the word, here its end

parts.note: to dun is to pester persistently, especially for payment
C is short for circa, about
to escape is to flee

explanation.surface: A plague is about to break out, and fleeing not fully is foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plague' reads as a noun about disease; it is the verb meaning to harass.
explanation.definitionFit: A dunce's cap was a cone-shaped hat put on a slow pupil, a classroom emblem of supposed stupidity.

clue.text: Visionary: "What's coming on Monday?"

parts.note: Monday brings the new year, a year remade

explanation.surface: A seer is asked to predict what Monday brings.
explanation.walkthrough: The theme's new YEAR is simply rearranged. Aery is a poetic variant of airy.
explanation.definitionFit: Aery means ethereal or lofty in imagination, so it fits visionary in the sense of fanciful.

clue.text: Improving old article by fellows in the centre of London

indicators.note: in places the preceding words inside the following ones

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old

indicators.note: the centre of a six-letter word is its middle pair of letters

parts.note: the middle two letters of London
the definite article
fellows are men

explanation.surface: An old item is restored by people in central London.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the article and fellows go inside the centre of London; the O for old stands in front of the whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the mend is an idiom for recovering, so it means improving, especially in health.

clue.text: Tea popular in group of cafes?

parts.note: cha (or char) is British slang for tea
something in is fashionable, popular

explanation.surface: Tea is the favourite drink across a coffee-shop franchise.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as one example: a chain can be of any shops.
explanation.definitionFit: A chain is a set of outlets under one owner, and cafes are one kind of business that forms them.

clue.text: Criticise work, largely empty, but a brilliant display

parts.note: to pan a show is to criticise it harshly
OP is short for opus, a work

indicators.note: empty means its inside is taken out, leaving only the outer letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of largely

explanation.surface: A critic slates a work as mostly hollow, yet showy.
explanation.definitionFit: A panoply is a splendid array or impressive collection, originally a full suit of armour.

clue.text: What's coming on Monday in a planet that's stormy? One may take a shot here

definitions.text: One may take a shot here

indicators.note: a stormy scene is turbulent, so these letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: Monday brings the new year
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what Monday brings on a planet wracked by storms.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a football box: the penalty area is the marked zone in front of goal where fouls give penalty kicks.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a penalty is a shot at goal from the spot inside the penalty area, so shots are taken there.

clue.text: Candidate I'm backing — nobody English will accept that

indicators.note: accepting something means taking it inside

parts.note: none means nobody

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the letters are read right to left

parts.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Someone backs a candidate but no English voter will go along with it.
explanation.definitionFit: A nominee is a person put forward for an office or award, which is what a candidate is.

clue.text: Local youngster displaying attitude in confines of Brechin

indicators.note: in places one item inside the other
the confines of a word are its boundaries, its first and last letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of Brechin
an air is a manner or attitude

explanation.surface: A child in Brechin, a Scottish town, shows some attitude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' signals a regional word: bairn is Scots and northern English for a child, fitting Brechin, a town in Angus.
explanation.definitionFit: Bairn is the Scottish dialect word for a child, so it is a youngster in local speech.

clue.text: Substantial obscurities about American criminals

indicators.note: about means around, wrapping the outer word round another

parts.note: big means substantial
mists obscure things
A is the abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: Large fogs envelop American lawbreakers.
explanation.definitionFit: Bigamists marry while already married, a crime, so they are a particular kind of criminal.

clue.text: Purging method adopted by guy with symptom of drunkenness

parts.note: cat is old jazz slang for a man or fellow

indicators.note: something adopted by another is taken into it

parts.note: hic represents a hiccup, a drunkard's stereotypical noise
an art is a skill or method

explanation.surface: A purge cure is taken up by a man who hiccups from drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Cathartic means providing emotional release or acting as a purgative, so it is purging.

clue.text: Stage performers arrive: audience primarily enthralled by loud noises

parts.note: to come is to arrive

indicators.note: something enthralled by another is held captive within it

parts.note: dins are loud noises

indicators.note: primarily points to the first letter only

parts.note: the first letter of audience

explanation.surface: Performers turn up, and the crowd is gripped by the racket.
explanation.definitionFit: Comedians are entertainers who perform comic routines on stage, so they are stage performers.

clue.text: Author and tense journalist: "What's coming on Monday?"

parts.note: T is the grammar abbreviation for tense
a hack is a journalist, often a mediocre one
Monday brings the new year

explanation.surface: A writer and an anxious reporter wonder about Monday.
explanation.walkthrough: The theme's new YEAR is rearranged as ERAY. William Makepeace Thackeray wrote Vanity Fair.
explanation.definitionFit: William Makepeace Thackeray was a Victorian novelist, an example of an author.

clue.text: Fellow offering information: article about return of thaw

parts.note: gen is British slang for information

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to thaw is to melt
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A man shares news: an item on the thaw coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' here means concerning, a link between the article and its subject, not a container.
explanation.definitionFit: Gentleman and fellow are both polite words for a man.

clue.text: Walk miles to be caught in ambush

indicators.note: being caught in something places it inside

parts.note: an ambush is a trap
M is the abbreviation for miles

explanation.surface: A hiker walks miles only to be ambushed.
explanation.definitionFit: To tramp is to walk heavily or trek a long way on foot.

clue.text: Male, working, observed to be well-off

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for male
a machine that is on is working
to eye something is to observe it

explanation.surface: A man in a job is seen to be prosperous.
explanation.definitionFit: Moneyed means having plenty of money, a synonym of wealthy or well-off.

clue.text: Note what's coming on Sunday, right? Not once

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for note
the day before New Year's Day is New Year's Eve, which fell on the Sunday
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone notes Sunday's event and asks whether it is right, then denies it.
explanation.walkthrough: A twist on the theme: Monday was New Year's Day, so Sunday brought its Eve.
explanation.definitionFit: Never means at no time at all, which is the sense of not once.

clue.text: Child's relatives hide

parts.note: a kid is a child, with the possessive kept
kin are relatives

explanation.surface: A child's family members go into hiding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hide' reads as a verb; it is the noun for an animal's skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Kidskin is leather made from a young goat's skin, and hide means an animal skin.

clue.text: Reflection of some skirtlike garment

indicators.note: a reflection is a mirror image, so the letters run the other way
some means a portion of the following words is used

parts.note: a run of letters inside this word

explanation.surface: Musing on the look of a garment that resembles a skirt.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is apt: a kilt is the skirtlike Scottish garment, so the surface describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A kilt is a pleated knee-length tartan garment traditionally worn by Scottish men.

clue.text: More precise governance taken up around college

indicators.note: in a down entry, taken up means read upwards
around means wrapping one word about another

parts.note: rein means control or rule, as in a free rein
C is the abbreviation for college

explanation.surface: Tighter rules are imposed on a college.
explanation.walkthrough: C goes inside REIN and the whole is then read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Nice can mean exact or finely discriminating, as in a nice distinction, so nicer means more precise.

clue.text: Claim provided by small investor

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
to aver is to claim or assert

explanation.surface: A small investor makes a claim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small investor' reads as one phrase, but small goes to the wordplay and investor alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A saver puts money aside in an account or fund, so a saver is a modest investor.

clue.text: Everybody with self-confidence gets mostly well-off, as implied in symbolic narrative

indicators.note: mostly means all but the last letter is kept

ego is a sense of self-esteem
rich means well-off

explanation.surface: Everyone confident ends up nearly rich, as a moral fable suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Allegoric means expressed through allegory, a story whose characters stand for hidden meanings.

clue.text: Set on climbing

indicators.note: in a down entry climbing means going upwards, so the word reads bottom to top

parts.note: on is the leg side in cricket, the half of the field behind the batsman's legs

explanation.surface: Fixed on going up.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the on side is also called the leg side, a standard crossword equivalence.
explanation.definitionFit: To gel is to set into a firm jelly, as a liquid does when cooling.

clue.text: Argon vapour very much behind source of some marine obstruction

indicators.note: the source of a word is where it begins, its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of some
Ar is argon's chemical symbol
a vapour is a gas
so means very, as in so much

explanation.surface: Gas from argon is largely to blame for something blocking the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' places the first three pieces after the S. The Sargasso Sea is a region of the Atlantic thick with floating seaweed.
explanation.definitionFit: Sargasso is seaweed that floats in dense mats, an obstruction to ships at sea.

clue.text: Performer, Poet Laureate: "What's coming on Monday?"

parts.note: PL abbreviates Poet Laureate
Monday brings the new year

explanation.surface: A performer and the Poet Laureate wonder about Monday.
explanation.walkthrough: The theme again: Monday brings the New Year, and 'new' tells you to rearrange the year's letters.
